lead: Selection takes n keys in any order and an integer k, and returns the k-th smallest. Searching takes sorted keys and one key x, and returns its position or reports it absent. Both discard data: one comparison decides which part can be thrown away. With p processors discarding different parts at once, the range shrinks faster and the steps fall. Databases use this for ORDER BY ... LIMIT and for medians; sorted-index lookups such as a railway timetable search use it too.
prereq: You need the PRAM cost model and the EREW/CRCW variants from Unit 1, plus broadcast from Chapter 2.3.

blocks.text: Selection takes n keys in any order and an integer k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n, and returns the key that would sit at position k if the keys were sorted. The keys are never sorted.
Sequential quickselect picks a pivot, splits by it, and recurses into the one side holding rank k. Expected time O(n); worst case O(n²), when every round drops one key.
The parallel version picks the pivot from p samples, so the split stays balanced for any input.

items: Processor j takes block j of about n/p keys and returns its median: the key at position ⌈m/2⌉ of its m keys.
Sort the p medians and take the one at position ⌈p/2⌉. That key is the pivot.
Broadcast the pivot to all processors.
Each processor counts keys below the pivot in its block. A prefix sum over the p counts gives the number of keys below the pivot; the pivot's rank is r = that count + 1.

If r = k, return the pivot. If k < r, keep the keys below the pivot, leave k unchanged, and repeat on the survivors. If k > r, keep the keys above the pivot, replace k by k − r, and repeat on the survivors.

blocks.text: T_p = Θ(log n) when p = n;  W = Θ(n) total work over all rounds
blocks.where: T_p is the parallel time with p processors, W is the total work (all processor steps added over all rounds), and n is the number of keys. The round sizes n, 3n/4, 9n/16, … sum to 4n. The product p · T_p = Θ(n log n) is only the processor-time product: it counts processors sitting idle in later rounds, so it is not the work.

blocks.text: The pivot is never extreme. At least ⌈p/2⌉ block medians are ≤ the pivot, and each of those blocks has at least ⌈m/2⌉ keys ≤ its own median, so at least (p/2)(m/2) = n/4 keys are ≤ the pivot. The same argument gives at least n/4 keys ≥ the pivot, so each round keeps at most 3n/4 keys and O(log n) rounds finish.

Ranking by enumeration avoids pivots: each key is compared with every other key in parallel and counts how many are smaller; the key with count k − 1 is the answer. Work O(n²), time O(n) with n processors.

sections.h3: Searching a sorted array with p processors

blocks.text: Searching takes a sorted array a[0..n−1] and a key x, and returns an index i with a[i] = x, or reports x absent. Binary search on one processor needs ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ comparisons in the worst case.

Plan A, blocks. Cut the array into p equal blocks, one per processor. Processor j binary searches its own block in ⌈log₂(n/p + 1)⌉ comparisons, so the block search costs Θ(log(n/p)). Reading the p per-block answers is a combine step: O(1) with a concurrent read, or O(log p) as a reduction. The full time is Θ(log(n/p) + log p) = Θ(log n).

Plan B, p-ary search. In one parallel step the p processors compare x with p − 1 probes that cut the range into p equal parts. Only the part between the two probes that bracket x survives, so the length falls by a factor p.
S(n, p) = ⌈log_p(n+1)⌉ = O(log n / log p)
blocks.where: S is the number of parallel steps, n is the number of sorted keys, p is the number of processors, and each step costs one broadcast of x plus p − 1 comparisons done at the same instant.

blocks.text: So p-ary search trades work for time: p − 1 comparisons per step make the total work O(p log_p n). Block split keeps the work near log(n/p), but its speedup stops growing once n/p becomes small.

spec.aria: The sorted array of 15 keys drawn twice: first with probes at indexes 3, 7 and 11 and the range 8 to 10 bracketed, then with 42 found at index 9; below, three binary-search comparisons.

examples.question: a = [3, 8, 12, 17, 21, 25, 29, 34, 38, 42, 47, 51, 55, 60, 66], n = 15, p = 4. (a) Find x = 42 by binary search and by 4-ary search, with the steps. (b) Select the k = 5 smallest key: give the block medians, the pivot, its rank, and how many keys are discarded.
steps: Binary search: mid = 7, a[7] = 34 < 42, so lo = 8. mid = 11, a[11] = 51 > 42, so hi = 10. mid = 9, a[9] = 42. Found at index 9 in 3 comparisons.
4-ary step 2: length 3, probes at 8 + 3//4 = 8 and 8 + 6//4 = 9, giving a[8] = 38 < 42 and a[9] = 42. Found at index 9 in 2 steps.
Block sizes: n//p = 3 with remainder 3, so the blocks hold 4, 4, 4, 3 keys: a[0..3], a[4..7], a[8..11], a[12..14]. Medians at position ⌈m/2⌉ are 8, 25, 42, 60.
Median of the four medians is the 2nd smallest, 25. Pivot = 25; 5 keys (3, 8, 12, 17, 21) are below it, so its rank is r = 6.
k = 5 < 6, so keep the 5 keys below 25 and discard the pivot with the 9 keys above it: 10 of 15 keys dropped. The 5th smallest of the survivors is 21.
examples.answer: x = 42 is at index 9, in 3 binary comparisons but only 2 parallel 4-ary steps; the k = 5 smallest key is 21, after one selection round discards 10 of the 15 keys.
examples.check:
a = [3,8,12,17,21,25,29,34,38,42,47,51,55,60,66]
n, p, x, k = len(a), 4, 42, 5

lo, hi, comps, bidx = 0, n-1, 0, -1
while lo <= hi:
    comps += 1
    mid = (lo+hi)//2
    if a[mid] == x:
        bidx = mid
        break
    lo, hi = (mid+1, hi) if a[mid] < x else (lo, mid-1)

lo, hi, steps, pidx = 0, n-1, 0, -1
while lo <= hi and pidx < 0:
    steps += 1
    m = hi-lo+1
    for j in range(p-1):
        i = lo + (j+1)*m//p
        if i > hi:
            break
        if a[i] == x:
            pidx = i
            break
        if a[i] < x:
            lo = i+1
        else:
            hi = i-1
            break

meds, s = [], 0
for j in range(p):
    sz = n//p + (j < n % p)
    meds.append(a[s + (sz+1)//2 - 1])
    s += sz
pivot = sorted(meds)[(p+1)//2 - 1]
rank = sum(v < pivot for v in a) + 1
kept = [v for v in a if v < pivot] if k < rank else [v for v in a if v > pivot]
if k > rank:
    k -= rank
print(bidx, comps, pidx, steps, pivot, n-len(kept), sorted(kept)[k-1])

traps: Quoting the parallel time alone. With p = n the time is Θ(log n) and the work is Θ(n); the product p · T_p = Θ(n log n) is not the work.
Mixing selection with searching. Selection reads unsorted keys and returns a value by rank; searching needs sorted keys and returns a position.
Using ⌈log₂(n+1)⌉ where p-ary search needs ⌈log_p(n+1)⌉, and forgetting that each p-ary step does p − 1 comparisons, not one.

Reporting only O(log(n/p)) for block-split search. Dropping the combine step leaves the p per-block answers unread, so no answer is reported; the combine costs O(1) with a concurrent read or O(log p) as a reduction, giving Θ(log(n/p) + log p) = Θ(log n) in total.
Calling the median of the block medians the true median. It is a pivot with rank near the middle, usually not n/2.

quiz.q: Define selection: its inputs and its output.
quiz.a: Inputs: n keys in any order and an integer k with 1 ≤ k ≤ n. Output: the key of rank k.

quiz.q: Why does the parallel selection method beat quickselect on the worst case?
quiz.a: The pivot is the median of p block medians, so at least n/4 keys lie on each side. No round drops fewer than a quarter of the keys, so the O(n²) extreme-pivot case cannot occur.

quiz.q: n = 63 sorted keys, p = 4. How many steps does 4-ary search take in the worst case, and how many comparisons in all?
quiz.a: ⌈log₄(63+1)⌉ = ⌈log₄ 64⌉ = 3 steps. Each step does p − 1 = 3 comparisons, so 3 × 3 = 9 comparisons.

quiz.q: n = 1000 sorted keys, p = 5, block-split search. Worst-case comparisons inside one block?
Compare block-split search and p-ary search on time and total work.
quiz.a: Block split: time Θ(log(n/p) + log p) = Θ(log n), work O(p log(n/p)); speedup saturates as n/p shrinks. p-ary: time O(log n / log p), work O(p log_p n); faster in time for large p, but the p − 1 comparisons per step raise the work.

quiz.q: Why must the pivot be broadcast before the partition step of parallel selection?
quiz.a: Every processor must split its block against the same key. Different pivots would make the block counts incomparable and the prefix-sum rank meaningless.

beyond: Not for the exam. numpy.partition uses introselect, which falls back to a median-of-medians pivot when recursion runs deep. Databases run top-k selection over shards and merge the per-shard ranks. GPU libraries run multi-way search over sorted arrays for joins and for learned index lookups.
